main_argument_chains.claim: Turbulent ocean reflection is weaker than the calm baseline.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Use the rough-surface branch and carry its loss into the link budget.

main_argument_chains.claim: A 100 W, 3 MHz calm-ocean signal is reported usable for six to seven hops under a 10 dB SNR threshold.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Treat the reported hop/distance as a scenario-bound threshold output.

main_argument_chains.claim: Smooth terrain is reported to retain more reflected power and hops than rugged terrain, while both are worse than sea.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Route terrain scenarios through a target-domain validation before operational use.

main_argument_chains.claim: A moving ship adds a 3.01 dB mismatch term and receives signal only in hop-specific intervals.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Combine interval geometry with ship trajectory and speed to compute service time.

main_argument_chains.claim: The paper's Summary and short note expose the same four-part requirement map to different audiences.
main_argument_chains.decision_consequence: Reuse the audience contract while preserving scenario and evidence strength.

warnings.warning: All 21 physical pages carry a red commercial watermark; physical page 8 repeats printed page 7 and printed pagination is offset thereafter.
Summary reverses the smooth/rugged first-reflection power assignment: its 'respectively' order conflicts with the body on physical page 16.
Summary assigns the ship coverage intervals to 24 MHz, whereas Figure 13 labels the shipboard curves as 3 MHz and Figure 14 gives no new frequency.
Figure 14 marks 2767 and 5786 km, while its prose and the Summary report 2676 and 5768 km.
Section 3.1.1 adopts seawater relative permittivity 7, but Table 1 later gives 70 for seawater.
Equation 28 prints -10 log10(100/Pmin)=+150.969 dB; the displayed ratio and sign would yield -150.969 dB.
The section calls itself Finite Element Analysis but supplies only a microfacet normal distribution; no finite-element mesh, element equation, assembly, boundary solve, or convergence appears.

Key citations appear mismatched: [5] after Blinn is an ionosphere paper, [6] after the CCIR formula is a vertical-dipole comment, [12] after cosmic noise is a lightning-field paper, and [13] after the material table is a lightning-process paper.
Equation 3 integrates a possibly complex amplitude coefficient directly, without magnitude, power square, angular probability weight, or normalization.
Equation 15 repeats the unnormalized complex-amplitude integral for turbulent loss, so the dB response interface remains ambiguous.
The prose calls theta_min the maximum incident angle; the symbol name, sentence, and integration role conflict.
The Figure 5 paragraph first identifies an angle relationship and then incorrectly says Figure 5 shows frequency; the frequency sweep is Figure 6.
Equation 29 lists each loss term once and never specifies per-hop accumulation, path segmentation, or reflection count, so Figures 10-13 cannot be regenerated from the printed ledger.
The 0.85 MUF heuristic is used as an operating point without computing MUF or connecting electron density and time/season to the frequency sweep.
The paper states the mismatch factor is always one-half for any circular-polarization arrangement; that value requires a particular ideal linear/circular pairing and matching conditions.
The claim that reflection points must not lie in one plane is not a geometric necessity, and the route/time conversion omits ship position, heading, speed, and remaining interval length.
Figure 16 is described as plus/minus 20 percent in epsilon_r and sigma, but its legend shows epsilon 70 to 56 and sigma 5 to 0.5, with no rise cases.
Sensitivity consists only of deterministic one-factor curves and one cross-medium contrast; no derivatives, interactions, uncertainty, convergence, or recommendation reversal are tested.
Equation 9 uses exponent e, while printed normalized Equations 11-12 drop that exponent from the dot-product factor.
The Blinn exponent e, geometrical attenuation G, angular domain, and calibration procedure are never defined.
The microfacet correction and the CCIR empirical correction are presented consecutively but never numerically reconciled, compared, or selected by a decision rule.

Direct Equation 14 evaluation at U=20 m/s, f=3 MHz, and theta=90 degrees gives h_w=2.04 m, rho about 0.96745, and only 0.144 dB of rho-only loss; the paper gives no integration convention that explains Figure 5's 10.578 dB endpoint.
Figures 7 and 11 label a 3-30 horizontal axis as Hz even though the paper and equations treat the range as MHz; Figure 6 correctly labels MHz.
The calm/turbulent first-reflection power ranges and the 0.5062 mW operating-point value lack the complete distance, angle, ionosphere, and loss parameter bundle needed for reproduction.
Equation 22 calls 20 log10(|E|/|E0|) an attenuation in dB even though it is negative for a decaying field; Equation 23 subtracts it, so terminology and sign convention are easy to reverse.
The high-frequency condition is printed as sigma/(omega sigma)<<1, which cancels sigma and is dimensionally invalid; the intended permittivity term is not shown.
Equation 25 introduces N, electron charge, collision frequency, and electron mass without defining or assigning them in the notation/data interface.
The unnumbered ionosphere path expression integrates A_2, but A_2 is undefined and differs from the preceding A_ion symbol.
The prose calls cosmic background radiation the dominant external noise, but the computation is a generic kTB thermal-noise proxy with no route-, time-, or receiver-specific noise model.
The unnumbered L_ion expression is a dimensionless exponential factor, while Equation 29 adds L_ion to dB losses without a conversion.
Figure 10's piecewise hop curves have no printed hop-distance geometry, curve-generation algorithm, or complete parameter ledger.
The claimed decline of maximum hops with frequency is not accompanied by a frequency-by-frequency threshold table or reproducible sweep.
The terrain branch only replaces material parameters and a roughness proxy; it does not model terrain diffraction, obstruction geometry, or validated scattering unique to land.
Figure 13 contains an n=5 segment while the text summarizes only 3 to 4 usable hops; the acceptance rule for partial curve segments is not stated.
Part III asks how long communication persists, but the paper supplies no ship speed, route, initial location, duration equation, or numerical time answer.

The Strengths section calls the rough method more accurate and universal without any benchmark data, error metric, external validation, random-repeat check, or comparison between its two roughness routes.

Equation 8 prints the P-M exponential with power -4, not +4: as omega approaches zero the exponential tends to one while omega^-5 diverges, contrary to the standard low-frequency cutoff; any +4 repair must be labeled as an emendation rather than source transcription.

At 3 MHz and about 2000 km, Equation 19 alone gives 108.013 dB of free-space loss, but Figure 10 plots total loss near 85 dB; Equations 22-23 and 29 can only add attenuation, and Figures 12-13 show the same below-FSPL defect.

Equations 3 and 15 integrate over theta_min to theta_max and therefore return a scalar for fixed inputs, while Figures 5 and 15-17 plot L_cal or L_tur as a point function of incidence angle without saying whether angle is an upper bound, a quadrature sample, or an unintegrated replacement.

Equations 11-13 switch from the defined omega_h to an undefined omega_n, and Equation 13 also introduces theta in its lower bound without defining how either variable maps to the preceding microplane geometry.
Table 1 gives dry-soil conductivity as 1.1e-3 to 2e-3 S/m but lists an average of 1e-3 S/m outside that range, weakening the terrain-transfer parameter ledger.

visualization_dispositions.analytical_purpose: Create a shared symbol-to-meaning interface for reflection, loss, frequency, material, and shipboard terms.
Show ionosphere/earth multi-hop geometry and motivate the propagation vocabulary.
Connect earth radius, ionosphere height, layer angles, and the angle bounds used by the calm-sea integral.
Compare simulated surface roughness for wind speeds 5, 10, 15, and 20 m/s.
Explain how local normals distribute reflected rays on a turbulent surface.
Contrast calm and rough surface attenuation over incidence angle at 3 MHz and U=20 m/s.
Show calm attenuation near constant and rough attenuation increasing across the stated frequency range.
Translate surface attenuation into first-reflection power ranges for calm and turbulent oceans.
Validate the logarithmic distance and frequency direction of Equation 19.
Provide non-specialists with the D/E/F layer structure used to motivate absorption.
Place a 151 dB threshold against hop-indexed calm-ocean loss curves.
Supply sea, freshwater, wet-soil, and dry-soil permittivity/conductivity inputs for cross-medium transfer.
Compare first-reflection power under two terrain roughness scenarios.
Compress the terrain comparison into threshold-based hop counts.
Show the additional loss scenario for a moving shipboard receiver over turbulent ocean.
Expose four hop-specific coverage ranges and the exclusion zones between them.
Show rough-surface attenuation over angle for U=5,10,15,20 m/s.
Use near-overlapping curves to argue local insensitivity under the plotted epsilon/sigma combinations.
Bound the local sensitivity claim with a visibly larger cross-medium response shift.
